name: Lacrosse ball / massage gun
lead: A lacrosse ball is a firm rubber ball used for self-massage against a wall or floor, and a massage gun is a handheld battery-powered percussive device that delivers rapid pulses, commonly 20 to 60 Hz, through interchangeable heads [1]. Both are used for muscle tension, soreness and trigger-point release, and people use them to keep muscles supple so that they can keep training, which is the route by which they connect to physique and posture goals.

The appearance link is mostly indirect. Looser muscles and better range of motion can support more consistent lifting and better movement, and in looksmaxxing circles a few users also apply the tools around the face and jaw, usually in discussions of bonesmashing or asymmetry. Research on percussive massage has examined recovery, flexibility and pain in small trials; a 2023 systematic review of 11 studies found short-term flexibility and range-of-motion gains but not performance gains in strength, balance or agility tasks [9]. A case report documented rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use, and another documented radial nerve injury after self-myofascial release with a lacrosse ball [3][12].

On looksmax.org, users discuss massage guns in connection with bonesmashing, a practice with no published support [5][6]. This article describes both tools, their history, the research that exists and the community discussion.

chain: Pressure or percussion on tight muscle
Short-term relief of stiffness and soreness, more range of motion
Easier, more consistent training and movement
angle.text: People use a lacrosse ball or massage gun to ease tight muscles and post-workout stiffness so they can keep training and moving freely. Some forum users also use massage guns around the face, a claim that remains untested [5][6][9].

paras: A lacrosse ball is a solid rubber sports ball, firmer than a foam roller or a tennis ball. In self-massage it is placed between a muscle and a wall or the floor and the body is moved over it, applying concentrated pressure to a small area such as the glutes, the shoulder blade region or the sole of the foot. Wikipedia classes foam rolling as a form of self-myofascial release, and lacrosse-ball work belongs to the same family of self-applied pressure techniques [20][21].

A massage gun is a handheld device in which a motor drives a head back and forth in a rapid, shallow stroke. Grokipedia describes frequencies of roughly 20 to 60 Hz and interchangeable heads [1]. Users hold the head against a muscle for short periods rather than kneading it by hand. A clinical commentary in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy covers the related field of vibration therapy [18].

Electric percussive massagers were patented in the mid-twentieth century, in 1955 and 1963 according to Grokipedia, and were sold mostly to physiotherapists and chiropractors until the 2010s [1]. Consumer models spread after Theragun, developed by chiropractor Jason Wersland, and Hyperice's Hypervolt in 2018, with social media and the COVID-19 period boosting sales [1].

Hand and tool-based massage itself has a long history. Wikipedia's article on massage traces written references to Egyptian, Assyrian, Chinese and Indian sources, notes that massage was televised on athletes at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, and became a core medical service for the US Olympic team in 1996 [19]. The concept of 'myofascial release' as a named therapy dates to the 1960s, when osteopath Robert Ward coined the term, and John Barnes popularised it through seminars for therapists, publishing a book on it in 1990 [21].

Self-applied tools followed the clinical techniques. Foam rollers and balls moved from physical-therapy settings into gyms and home use, and T Nation training logs and forum posts show lifters mentioning a lacrosse ball or foam roller for stiffness and mobility work [22][23][24].

In athletic and gym settings, users apply the lacrosse ball or massage gun before training to warm up, after training to ease soreness, or between sessions on stiff areas. In T Nation threads, lifters describe breaking out the lacrosse ball and doing some stretching on an evening before a hard session, and one forum member contrasts a massage gun with a cheaper 'general purpose massager' that does a similar job [22][24]. A 2025 pilot study compared a Theragun with foam rolling and a no-activation control, and reported that percussion improved hamstring flexibility more than the other conditions [13].

A 2025 crossover study of 35 healthy adults compared eight different massage-gun protocols for lower-body flexibility, noting that published protocols are heterogeneous [15]. This variation is one reason that research results differ between studies.

The 2023 systematic review searched six databases, screened 281 records and included 11 studies, most of moderate risk of bias. It reported that massage guns may improve flexibility in several muscle groups and aid short-term range of motion and recovery, such as reduced stiffness after fatigue, whereas strength, balance, acceleration, agility and explosive performance were not improved and sometimes reduced; contraction time, perceived exertion and lactate showed no differences [9].

Wikipedia's foam roller article reports short-term range-of-motion gains but unknown long-term effects, and cites a 2021 meta-analysis that supports foam rolling as a warm-up more than a recovery tool, although post-exercise rolling reduced perceived muscle pain [20]. Its myofascial release article cites a review finding that self-myofascial release may reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness, may increase range of motion and appears not to harm performance, with optimal timing and duration unclear [21]. The American Cancer Society and a 2013 systematic review, cited there, describe limited or mixed evidence for broader clinical claims [21].

A 5-minute massage gun application was tested for perceptual and physical recovery in active adults, in a study whose authors called the devices new and under-researched [2]. A trial examined percussive massage with and without heat on plantar flexor (calf) muscle properties [7]. A trial of 30 college students compared six minutes of massage gun treatment with a muscle energy technique for hamstring shortness; both groups improved sit-and-reach scores and muscle strength [14]. A crossover trial in 18 active students compared a Theragun with foam rolling and no activation for hamstring flexibility and muscle performance [13]. A randomised trial in 37 physically active men examined percussive massage on quadriceps cross-sectional area, strength and late muscle pain after a fatigue protocol, a setting in which the authors note empirical evidence is limited [17]. A 2024 study examined percussive massage for symptoms of eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage [16].

A self-myofascial release study of the superficial back line reported improved sit-and-reach distance [8]. A randomized trial tested local vibration therapy in cervical disc herniation for pain and function [4]. A case report described using a lacrosse ball with compression tack and flossing for adolescent Achilles tendinopathy [10]. A clinical commentary reviews vibration therapy more broadly [18]. No studies found testing either tool for facial structure or bone changes.

A 2021 case report in Physical Therapy described rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use [3]. A 2023 article titled 'Massage Gun Ophthalmopathy' in the journal Ophthalmology discusses eye problems associated with massage gun use [11]. A 2026 case report in Annals of Plastic Surgery describes a 44-year-old woman who developed a radial nerve compression injury at the upper arm after self-myofascial release with a lacrosse ball; she underwent surgical decompression and had regained partial nerve function at 18-month follow-up [12].

Forum users note the heads could harm the eye area at high settings [6]. Wikipedia's massage article lists general contraindications for massage, including deep vein thrombosis in the treated limb, caution for people taking anticoagulants, and caution with osteoporosis, fractures or fever [19].

Users on looksmax.org ask whether bonesmashing combined with a massage gun has any effect. One thread opens with a user who has been combining the two for three days and says they found no information in the forum; others reply jokingly [5]. In another thread a poster says the soft attachments are unlikely to change bone but may help asymmetry, and warns that the maximum setting could injure an eye [6].
Outside the bonesmashing discussion, the tools appear in the general fitness-forum context of mobility, soreness and recovery [22][23][24].

Massage guns differ in stroke length, speed settings, battery life, head shapes and noise. Grokipedia notes that devices come with interchangeable heads [1]. A T Nation member notes that cheaper general-purpose massagers are sold as alternatives to branded guns [22].

lore.intro: Massage guns appear in looksmaxxing threads mainly alongside bonesmashing and muscle-tension discussions; lacrosse balls and foam rollers appear in lifting forums as mobility tools. [5][6][22][24]

claims.claim: A massage gun can reduce facial asymmetry
claims.believers: One forum poster says using a massage gun could decrease the chance of asymmetries, while stating the soft heads would not create new bone [6].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined massage guns for facial asymmetry.

claims.claim: Bonesmashing with a massage gun changes facial bones
claims.believers: Users ask whether the combination works, noting few answers in the forum [5].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this; the studies found examine muscle recovery and flexibility, not bone remodelling [2][9].

claims.claim: Massage guns speed muscle recovery and mobility
claims.believers: Lifters describe using guns and balls to manage stiffness and soreness between sessions [22][24].
claims.experts: A 2023 systematic review found short-term flexibility, range-of-motion and recovery benefits across 11 studies, with most at moderate risk of bias [9]. A 2024 study of eccentric muscle damage and a 2026 trial in active men examine soreness outcomes [16][17].

claims.claim: Massage guns improve strength and athletic performance
claims.believers: Percussive massage is often used as a pre-workout warm-up tool in gym settings, in the hope of better performance.
claims.experts: The 2023 review reported no improvement, and sometimes reductions, in strength, balance, acceleration, agility and explosive tasks, and recommended against use for those goals [9]. A 2025 pilot study compared percussion with foam rolling on flexibility, reactive and explosive strength and muscular endurance [13].

claims.claim: Foam rollers and lacrosse balls release fascia and improve flexibility
claims.believers: Proponents of myofascial release say that pressure relaxes contracted muscle and improves circulation [21].
claims.experts: Reviews cited on Wikipedia, including a 2019 review and a 2021 meta-analysis, report short-term range-of-motion gains and some effect on perceived soreness, with optimal dosing unclear and long-term effects unknown [20][21].

claims.claim: Self-massage with a hard ball or a gun is risk-free
claims.believers: Gym forums commonly treat the tools as routine accessories [22][23].
claims.experts: Case reports describe rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use, radial nerve palsy after lacrosse-ball self-myofascial release, and an ophthalmology paper on massage gun eye injury [3][11][12].

card.summary: Self-massage tools for muscle tension; research is limited to recovery and mobility, with nothing on looks.
card.aka: Percussive massager, Theragun-style, trigger point ball
card.note: A rhabdomyolysis case report exists; bonesmashing use is untested.

quick.overview:
A lacrosse ball is pressed against a wall or floor for self-massage, while a massage gun hammers tissue with fast pulses. Both target muscle knots and soreness.

Studies cover recovery and mobility. Nothing has tested them for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Pressure or percussion on soft tissue, intended to ease tension, aid range of motion and reduce soreness.[1][2]
quick.risks: A case report links massage gun use to rhabdomyolysis.[3] Regulatory status is that of a consumer wellness device.
